key_insight: A pre-registered, investigator-blinded randomized controlled trial (n=153) quantified how mid‑2025 large language models affect novices performing lab-relevant biology tasks, providing empirical evidence about LLM assistance on human performance rather than model-only benchmarks.
problem_solved: Bridges the gap between model benchmark performance and real-world human outcomes by measuring whether LLMs actually improve (or change) novices' ability to carry out tasks that collectively model viral reverse‑genetics workflows.
method: Pre-registered, investigator-blinded randomized controlled trial conducted June–August 2025 with 153 participants.
Participants performed a suite of lab-relevant tasks modeling viral reverse genetics; compared LLM-assisted vs. unassisted conditions using objective performance metrics and predefined endpoints.
Statistical analysis measured differences in task success, error rates, and decision patterns to assess the net effect of LLM assistance on novice performance.
impact: Provides actionable empirical evidence for AI/ML practitioners, policymakers, and safety teams about how LLM capabilities translate to human behavior in sensitive domains—informing model deployment, guardrails, and risk assessments.
visual_elements: Trial flow diagram showing randomization, blinding, and intervention vs control arms
Bar/violin plots comparing performance metrics (success rate, error rate) between LLM-assisted and control groups
Timeline showing study period, participant flow (enrollment → tasks → evaluation), and pre-registration marker
Risk/benefit matrix or icon set summarizing implications for safety, policy, and model deployment
paper_title: Measuring Mid-2025 LLM-Assistance on Novice Performance in Biology
paper_authors: Shen Zhou Hong, Alex Kleinman, Alyssa Mathiowetz, Adam Howes, Julian Cohen
